title: A Neuroscientist on Consciousness
description: Four extracts in which neuroscientists discuss what consciousness is and whether science can explain it.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Mai, interviewing a neuroscientist, Dr Adeyemi.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Dr Adeyemi, you've spent thirty years studying the brain, and yet you describe consciousness as the thing that keeps you humble. Why?

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: Because we can explain a great deal about the brain without touching the central mystery. We know which regions light up when you see red, and we can predict, rather well, what a person will report. But why should any of that activity feel like something from the inside? That's the question philosophers call the hard problem, and I confess that no experiment I've run has made it feel any easier.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Some of your colleagues say the problem is an illusion, that once we explain every function, nothing will be left to explain.

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: I respect that position, and I used to lean towards it. The trouble is that it asks me to deny the one thing I know with certainty, which is that I am having an experience right now. It seems a high price to pay for tidiness.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: So where does a scientist even begin?

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: Modestly. Rather than asking what consciousness is, we ask what differs in the brain when a stimulus is consciously perceived and when it is not. You can show someone a faint image so that it is sometimes noticed and sometimes missed, and then compare the brain activity in the two cases. It's unglamorous work, but it narrows the search.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: And what have you found?

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: That conscious perception tends to involve a sudden, widespread burst of activity across the brain, whereas unconscious processing stays local. Whether that burst creates the experience or merely accompanies it is exactly where the argument begins.

parts.title: Part 2 · A lecture on theories
parts.intro: You will hear a neuroscientist, Dr Karlsson, describing rival theories of consciousness.

script.speaker: Dr Karlsson
script.text: At the moment, the field is dominated by a handful of rival theories, and it would be dishonest to pretend that any has won. The first I will mention is the global workspace theory. It likens the mind to a theatre in which a small spotlight picks out one piece of information and broadcasts it to the whole audience of specialised processes. What you are conscious of is simply what has entered the spotlight.

script.speaker: Dr Karlsson
script.text: The second, integrated information theory, takes the opposite approach. It begins not with the brain but with the experience itself, and asks what any physical system would need to have in order to support it. Its answer is a particular kind of interconnectedness, and the controversial consequence is that consciousness might exist in places we would never expect, even in simple devices.

script.speaker: Dr Karlsson
script.text: A third family of ideas holds that consciousness is the brain's best guess about what is causing its sensory signals. On this view, perception is a kind of controlled hallucination, constantly corrected by incoming data. Some of the most vivid support comes from illusions, where the brain stubbornly sees what it expects rather than what is there.

script.speaker: Dr Karlsson
script.text: Naturally, these theories make different predictions, and recently several research groups agreed to test them against each other in a large collaborative project. What I admire is that the leaders of each theory publicly committed in advance to say what result would count against them. The outcome was mixed, with each camp finding aspects that fit and aspects that did not.

script.speaker: Dr Karlsson
script.text: Some people read that as failure. I read it as science behaving properly. A field that can be embarrassed by its own data is a field that is learning, and I would sooner have an honest stalemate than a premature victory.

parts.title: Part 3 · Patients and animals
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Daniel, talking to a researcher, Dr Nguyen, about consciousness in patients and animals.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Dr Nguyen, you work with patients who appear unresponsive after severe brain injury. How can you tell whether anyone is still in there?

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: It's one of the most difficult questions in medicine, and for a long time we relied on behaviour alone. If a patient did not respond, we assumed that nobody was home. We now know that is sometimes wrong. In a famous set of studies, patients who showed no outward sign of awareness were asked to imagine playing tennis, and their brain scans showed the same pattern as healthy volunteers doing so.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That must have been astonishing.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: It was sobering, frankly. Families had been told for years that their relative could not hear them. Of course, a result like that is only the beginning, because we need much better ways of detecting awareness than asking someone to imagine a sport. Some teams now stimulate the brain with a magnetic pulse and measure how the echo spreads, which doesn't depend on the patient doing anything at all.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And what about animals? Surely they are conscious too.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Many scientists believe so, and a group of researchers signed a declaration saying that mammals and birds possess the neural machinery for experience. I'd add a caution, though. The difficulty is that we have only our own experience as a guide, and we risk either projecting it onto creatures that lack it or denying it to those who have it. Neither mistake is harmless.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Why does the answer matter?

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Because it determines how we treat them. If an octopus can suffer, then how we farm and cook it is an ethical question, not merely a culinary one. And I would rather we err on the side of kindness.

parts.title: Part 4 · A closing essay
parts.intro: You will hear a neuroscientist reflecting on what understanding consciousness might change.

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: People sometimes ask me whether a complete theory of consciousness would spoil the mystery. I have heard the worry that explaining the mind would make it ordinary, in the way that critics once said a rainbow lost its magic when it was explained as refracted light. My experience has been the reverse. The more I learn, the more astonished I become.

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: What I do worry about is the practical side. Within a few decades we may build machines that talk about feelings with great fluency. Whether they feel anything is a question we are currently unprepared to answer, and fluency is a poor guide. A very convincing performance of distress is not the same as distress.

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: I find myself caught between two mistakes. If we dismiss the possibility that artificial systems might one day be conscious, we risk ignoring suffering that we ourselves have created. If we grant consciousness too readily, we may be manipulated by clever software and waste sympathy that real creatures need. A good theory is therefore not an academic luxury. It is a moral tool.

script.speaker: Dr Adeyemi
script.text: Finally, a personal note. Studying the brain has made me gentler. When I think that each person I meet is the centre of a private universe I can never enter, I find it harder to be impatient. That is not a scientific conclusion, I admit, but it is the most valuable thing the work has given me.

questions.text: Why does Dr Adeyemi say consciousness keeps him humble?
options: Experiments on the brain have become too expensive to run
Philosophers have already solved the hard problem
He has failed to find any brain activity linked to seeing red
Explaining brain functions leaves experience itself unexplained
questions.explanation: He says we can explain much without touching why activity should feel like something.

evidence.quote: But why should any of that activity feel like something from the inside?

questions.text: What is his view of the idea that the hard problem is an illusion?
options: He has never taken it seriously and has always rejected it
He has always supported it and still holds that view
He once leaned towards it but now finds it too costly
He thinks it is obviously right, since functions explain all
questions.explanation: He used to lean towards it but says it asks him to deny experience, a high price for tidiness.

evidence.quote: It seems a high price to pay for tidiness.

questions.text: What does the experiment with faint images compare?
options: Brain activity when a faint image is noticed or missed
Eyesight in different people shown the same faint image
Brain activity in people who are asleep and awake
Responses to images shown in colour and in black and white
questions.explanation: It compares brain activity when a faint image is noticed and when it is missed.

evidence.quote: compare the brain activity in the two cases

questions.text: Why is the burst of activity finding still disputed?
options: It is unclear if it causes experience or just accompanies it
It was never repeated by other research teams
It has been observed only in animals, not in humans
It stays local to one region, so it proves little about awareness
questions.explanation: He says whether it creates the experience or merely accompanies it is where the argument begins.

evidence.quote: Whether that burst creates the experience or merely accompanies it

questions.text: According to Dr Adeyemi, what characterises unconscious processing?
options: It is much easier to measure in the laboratory
It produces a sudden burst of activity everywhere
It spreads widely across the whole of the brain
It stays local rather than spreading across the brain
questions.explanation: He says conscious perception involves a widespread burst, whereas unconscious processing stays local.

evidence.quote: whereas unconscious processing stays local

questions.text: What does Dr Karlsson say about the state of the field?
options: No single theory has won out yet
All of the theories now broadly agree
Consciousness has at last been explained
Global workspace theory has been confirmed

evidence.quote: it would be dishonest to pretend that any has won

questions.text: What does global workspace theory compare the mind to?
options: A computer network of processors
A river fed by many streams
A theatre with a spotlight
A library with many readers

questions.text: What controversial consequence does integrated information theory have?
options: Consciousness might exist in simple devices
Brains are unnecessary for any kind of thought
Only humans are able to be conscious
Consciousness is an illusion of the brain
questions.explanation: She says consciousness might exist in places we would not expect, even in simple devices.

evidence.quote: even in simple devices

questions.text: Why does she say she admires the leaders of each theory?
options: They agreed with one another on every point
They refused to take part in the joint project
They stated in advance what would count against them
They won the argument over the rival theories
questions.explanation: They publicly committed in advance to say what result would count against them.

evidence.quote: publicly committed in advance to say what result would count against them

questions.text: What is Dr Karlsson's attitude towards the mixed outcome of the joint project?
options: She sees it as science working as it should
She regards it as a failure of the whole field
She is angry with the leaders of each camp
She thinks the project was a waste of time
questions.explanation: She says she reads it as science behaving properly.

evidence.quote: I read it as science behaving properly.

questions.text: What did the scans of unresponsive patients show?
options: Random patterns that doctors could not interpret
Damage spread across the whole of the brain
No activity at all in the relevant regions
The same patterns as healthy people imagining tennis

questions.text: How does Dr Nguyen describe her reaction to that result?
options: Disappointing, because the scans were unclear
Unsurprising, because doctors had long suspected it
Encouraging, because the patients had recovered
Sobering, because families had been told otherwise

questions.text: Why does she mention a magnetic pulse?
options: It cures some kinds of severe brain injury
It replaces brain scans in studies of healthy volunteers
It detects awareness without any effort from the patient
It works only on animals, not on human patients

questions.text: What has studying the brain done for him personally?
options: It has made him lonely among his colleagues
It has made him more sceptical of science
It has made him wealthier than he expected
It has made him gentler and more patient
questions.explanation: He says studying the brain has made him gentler and less impatient.
